claim: 770 plastid-targeted proteins are conserved across the ochrophytes.
source: Here, we identify and characterise 770 plastid-targeted proteins that are conserved across the ochrophytes, a major group of algae including diatoms, pelagophytes and kelps, that possess plastids derived from red algae.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of conserved plastid-targeted proteins identified in the study.

claim: Ochrophytes possess plastids derived from red algae.
source: Here, we identify and characterise 770 plastid-targeted proteins that are conserved across the ochrophytes, a major group of algae including diatoms, pelagophytes and kelps, that possess plastids derived from red algae.
evidence: The abstract states that ochrophyte plastids are derived from red algae, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: 25% of phylogenetically tractable nucleus-encoded proteins in the ancestral ochrophyte plastid proteome derive from green algae.
source: We show that the ancestral ochrophyte plastid proteome was an evolutionary chimera, with 25% of its phylogenetically tractable nucleus-encoded proteins deriving from green algae.
evidence: The abstract provides a specific percentage based on phylogenetic analysis of the dataset.

claim: The ancestral ochrophyte plastid proteome was an evolutionary chimera.
source: We show that the ancestral ochrophyte plastid proteome was an evolutionary chimera, with 25% of its phylogenetically tractable nucleus-encoded proteins deriving from green algae.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the plastid proteome as chimeric based on the diverse evolutionary origins of its proteins.

claim: Functional mixing of host and plastid proteomes through dual-targeting is an ancestral feature of plastid evolution.
source: We additionally show that functional mixing of host and plastid proteomes, such as through dual-targeting, is an ancestral feature of plastid evolution.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on analysis of dual-targeted proteins in the dataset.

claim: There is a phylogenetic signal from the pelagophyte/dictyochophyte lineage in plastid-targeted proteins from haptophytes.
source: Finally, we detect a clear phylogenetic signal from one ochrophyte subgroup, the lineage containing pelagophytes and dictyochophytes, in plastid-targeted proteins from another major algal lineage, the haptophytes.
evidence: The abstract reports detection of phylogenetic signal based on analysis of haptophyte plastid-targeted proteins.

claim: The phylogenetic signal from pelagophytes/dictyochophytes in haptophytes may represent a serial endosymbiosis event deep in eukaryotic evolutionary history.
source: This may represent a possible serial endosymbiosis event deep in eukaryotic evolutionary history.
evidence: The abstract proposes this interpretation of the phylogenetic signal, indicating it is speculative.

claim: All but one characterized group of photosynthetic eukaryotes possess plastids resulting from a single ancient endosymbiosis of a beta-cyanobacterium by an ancestor of the archaeplastid lineage.
source: All but one characterized group of photosynthetic eukaryotes possess plastids resulting from a single ancient endosymbiosis of a beta-cyanobacterium by an ancestor of the archaeplastid lineage (consisting of green algae and plants, red algae, and glaucophytes) (Dorrell and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Photosynthesis has spread outside of the archaeplastids through secondary, tertiary, or more complex endosymbiosis events.
source: Photosynthesis has subsequently spread outside of the archaeplastids through secondary, tertiary, or more complex endosymbiosis events.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field of plastid evolution.

claim: The CASH lineages (cryptomonads, alveolates, stramenopiles, and haptophytes) are the most ecologically successful lineages with plastids derived from secondary or more complex endosymbioses of a red alga.
source: By far the most ecologically successful of these lineages are those that possess plastids derived from secondary or more complex endosymbioses of a red alga (Dorrell and Smith, 2011; Baurain et al., 2010; Stiller et al., 2014). These are the 'CASH lineages', consisting of photosynthetic members of the cryptomonads, alveolates (such as dinoflagellates), stramenopiles (also referred to as heterokonts) and haptophytes (Dorrell and Smith, 2011; Baurain et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Diatoms are major primary producers in the ocean.
source: The ochrophytes include the diatoms, which are major primary producers in the ocean (Bowler et al., 2010; Armbrust et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations and is well-established knowledge about diatom ecology.

claim: Multicellular kelps serve as spawning grounds for marine animals.
source: multicellular kelps, which serve as spawning grounds for marine animals (Cock et al., 2010)
evidence: This ecological role is supported by citation.

claim: Some pelagophytes are known to form harmful blooms.
source: the pelagophytes, microscopic algae of which some are known to form harmful blooms (Gobler et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The stramenopiles contain many aplastidic and non-photosynthetic lineages that diverge at the base of the ochrophytes.
source: The stramenopiles also contain many aplastidic and non-photosynthetic lineages (e.g., oomycetes), which diverge at the base of the ochrophytes and play important roles as pathogens and in microbial food webs (Aleoshin et al., 2016; Derelle et al., 2016)
evidence: This phylogenetic relationship is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Many plastid-targeted proteins are not derived from the genomes of the corresponding endosymbiont lineage.
source: Previous studies have shown that many plastid-targeted proteins are not derived from the genomes of the corresponding endosymbiont lineage (Curtis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Plastid-targeting sequences in different ochrophytes are relatively well conserved, enabling in silico prediction.
source: Firstly, plastid-targeting sequences in different ochrophytes are relatively well conserved, enabling in silico prediction of plastid-targeted proteins from a wide range of different species (Gruber et al., 2015; Gschloessl et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on plastid-targeting prediction tools.

claim: Plastid-targeting sequences within archaeplastid lineages are extremely variable.
source: in contrast to plastid-targeting sequences within archaeplastid lineages, which are extremely variable (Fuss et al., 2013; Suzuki and Miyagishima, 2010).
evidence: This contrast is supported by citations.

claim: Eleven complete ochrophyte genomes are available.
source: compared to other CASH lineages (haptophytes, cryptomonads, and dinoflagellates), ochrophytes represent an extremely well characterised system for experimental and bioinformatic investigation, with (to date) eleven complete genomes
evidence: This is a factual statement about available genomic resources at the time of the study.

claim: Transcriptome libraries are available for over 150 ochrophyte species through MMETSP and other sources.
source: and transcriptome libraries available for over 150 species through MMETSP (the Marine Microeukaryote Transcriptome Sequencing Project) and through other sources (Mock et al., 2017; Keeling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about available transcriptomic resources, supported by citations.

claim: Reliable transformation and manipulation strategies are available for Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
source: Reliable transformation and other manipulation strategies are also available for multiple species, such as the model diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum (Siaut et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2007; Radakovits et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: It is currently not known when the ochrophyte plastid was acquired.
source: It is currently not known when the ochrophyte plastid was acquired: whether it originated recently, predates the radiation of aplastidic stramenopile relatives (Stiller et al., 2014; Aleoshin et al., 2016; Derelle et al., 2016), or was acquired prior to the divergence of stramenopiles from their closest relatives, the alveolates (Janouskovec et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement acknowledges uncertainty in the field, with citations to different hypotheses.

claim: It has been proposed that the ancestor of ochrophytes once possessed a green algal endosymbiont that was subsequently replaced via serial endosymbiosis of a red algal-derived plastid.
source: It has additionally been proposed, based on the presence of large numbers of genes of putative green algal origin in diatom genomes (Frommolt et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2006), that the ancestor of ochrophytes once possessed a green algal endosymbiont, which was subsequently replaced via the serial endosymbiosis of a red algal-derived plastid (Dorrell and Smith, 2011; Moustafa et al., 2009).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hypothesis of a green algal endosymbiont in ochrophyte ancestors remains controversial.
source: This hypothesis remains controversial (Ku et al., 2015; Woehle et al., 2011; Deschamps and Moreira, 2012)
evidence: The controversy is indicated by citations to papers challenging the hypothesis.

claim: One recent study proposed that haptophytes possess plastids acquired via the endosymbiosis of an ochrophyte.
source: One recent study proposed that haptophytes possess plastids acquired via the endosymbiosis of an ochrophyte (Stiller et al., 2014)
evidence: This proposal is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The exact identity of the ochrophyte endosymbiotic donor to haptophytes remains unresolved.
source: although the exact identity of this endosymbiotic acquisition remain unresolved.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge despite the proposal.

claim: The ancestral ochrophyte plastid-targeted proteome contains 770 proteins from a range of different sources.
source: We show that this ancestral plastid-targeted proteome was an evolutionary mosaic, containing 770 proteins from a range of different sources.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the dataset.

claim: The ochrophyte plastid was acquired late in stramenopile evolution, following the divergence of extant aplastidic relatives.
source: Our dataset indicates that the ochrophyte plastid was acquired late in stramenopile evolution, following the divergence of extant aplastidic relatives
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from analysis of the dataset.

claim: Plastid-targeted proteins of green algal origin played a significant role in the origin of the ochrophyte plastid.
source: that plastid-targeted proteins of green algal origin played a significant role in its origin
evidence: This is inferred from the proportion of green algal proteins in the dataset.

claim: There has been bidirectional integration of the biology of the ochrophyte host and plastid proteomes.
source: and that there has been bidirectional integration of the biology of the ochrophyte host and plastid proteomes, such as the ancient recruitment of proteins from both host and endosymbiont to dually support the biology of the plastid and mitochondria.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the identification of dual-targeted proteins.

claim: There is evidence for an ancient endosymbiosis of a pelagophyte/dictyochophyte ancestor by a common ancestor of the haptophytes.
source: Finally, we show evidence for an ancient endosymbiosis of a specific ochrophyte lineage, an ancestor of the pelagophytes and dictyochophytes, by a common ancestor of the haptophytes
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of haptophyte plastid-targeted proteins.

claim: The discrepancy between haptophyte plastid proteome and genome origins reveals a possible serial endosymbiosis event early in haptophyte evolution.
source: which we propose- based on discrepancies between the origins of the haptophyte plastid proteome and genome- reveals a possible serial endosymbiosis event early in haptophyte evolution, preceding the origins of the current haptophyte plastid.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed discrepancy.

claim: Molecular divergence estimates place the ochrophytes as diverging from the oomycetes no more than 90 million years prior to the radiation of ochrophyte lineages.
source: The relatively late origin of the ochrophyte plastid is particularly interesting as molecular divergence estimates place the ochrophytes as diverging from the oomycetes no more than 90 million years prior to the radiation of ochrophyte lineages (Brown and Sorhannus, 2010; Matari and Blair, 2014).
evidence: This is based on molecular clock estimates from cited studies.

claim: The ancestral ochrophyte plastid proteome dataset represents some of the earliest proteins to support the ochrophyte plastid following its endosymbiotic uptake.
source: Assuming that these estimates are reliable, our dataset represents some of the earliest proteins to support the ochrophyte plastid following its endosymbiotic uptake.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of molecular clock estimates and the ancestral nature of the dataset.

claim: 106 of the inferred ancestral HPPGs include a P. tricornutum protein with prior experimental plastid localization or unambiguous plastid function.
source: 106 of our inferred ancestral HPPGs include a P. tricornutum protein with prior experimental plastid localization, or unambiguous plastid function (Figure 1, panel D)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1, panel D.

claim: Ten proteins were selected for experimental localisation based on having only non-plastid annotations in the first 50 BLAST hits against NCBI nr database excluding ochrophytes.
source: We selected ten proteins for experimental localisation (Figure 2, panel A; Table S5 [Dorrell et al., 2016]). These were chosen on the basis of having only non-plastid annotations on the first 50 BLAST hits against the NCBI nr database excluding ochrophytes
evidence: The selection criteria are explicitly stated and referenced to Figure 2 and Table S5.

claim: All ochrophyte protein sequences within each selected HPPG alignment had a well conserved central domain and a highly variable N-terminal domain of 30-50 amino acids containing an ASAFAP motif.
source: In each case, all of the ochrophyte protein sequences within the alignment had a well conserved central domain, and a highly variable N-terminal domain of between 30 and 50 amino acids containing an ASAFAP motif, consistent with a conserved plastid targeting sequence (Gruber et al., 2015) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with citation to support the interpretation.

claim: All ten experimentally tested proteins showed at least partial targeting to the plastid in P. tricornutum.
source: However, in all cases the proteins tested were at least partially targeted to the plastid.
evidence: This is the summary result of the experimental localization studies.

claim: Heterologous expression of five proteins from G. foliaceum and N. gaditana in P. tricornutum showed plastid-localized GFP fluorescence similar to P. tricornutum constructs.
source: We expressed these constructs in P. tricornutum (Figure 2, panel B; Figure 2—figure supplement 6), and, in each case, detected plastid-localized GFP fluorescence similar to the patterns observed with the P. tricornutum gene constructs.
evidence: This experimental result is stated and shown in figures.

claim: Of 263 HPPGs resolved by combined analysis, 149 (57%) were of red algal origin.
source: Of the 263 HPPGs that were resolved from the combined analysis, 149 (57%) were of red algal, i.e. endosymbiont origin (Figure 3, panel A; Table S4- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phylogenetic and BLAST analysis.

claim: 67 HPPGs (25% of 263 resolved) were of green algal origin.
source: The most significant of these lineages was green algae (67 HPPGs, 25%)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: 26 HPPGs (10% of 263 resolved) were of aplastidic stramenopile origin.
source: followed by aplastidic stramenopiles (26 HPPGs, 10%)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: 21 HPPGs (8% of 263 resolved) were of prokaryotic origin.
source: and prokaryotes (21 HPPGs, 8%) (Figure 3, panel A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: None of the HPPGs were clearly assigned to other eukaryotes or to viruses.
source: None of the HPPGs were clearly assigned to other eukaryotes or to viruses, consistent with previous assertions that these lineages have contributed very little to ochrophyte evolution (Bowler et al., 2008) (Figure 3, panel A).
evidence: This negative result is stated and consistent with cited previous work.

claim: The majority (20/26) of ochrophyte HPPGs with aplastidic stramenopile origins specifically resolved as sister-group to oomycetes.
source: First, we noted that the majority (20/26) of the ochrophyte HPPGs with aplastidic stramenopile origins specifically resolved as a sister-group to oomycetes, as opposed to the deeper-branching labyrinthulomycetes or slopalinids (Figure 3, panel B; Table S4- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Only one BLAST top hit and four trees of aplastidic stramenopile-origin HPPGs showed a deeper red algal affinity.
source: However, only one BLAST top hit and four trees showed a deeper red algal affinity (Figure 3, panel B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The proportions of red algal affinity in aplastidic stramenopile-origin HPPGs are significantly smaller than expected based on the overall dataset (chi-squared test, p≤0.01).
source: These proportions are significantly smaller than the proportions of ochrophyte proteins of red origin in the entire ancestral HPPG dataset (expected frequencies: 9.54 BLAST top hits, 10.7 sister-groups; chi-squared test, p≤0.01; Figure 3, panels A, B).
evidence: This statistical test supports the conclusion of late plastid origin.

claim: For the majority of green HPPGs (40/67), an orthologue was identified in at least four of the five major red algal sub-categories.
source: For the majority of our green HPPGs (40/67), an orthologue was identified in at least four of the five major red algal sub-categories considered (cyanidiales, bangophytes and florideophytes, compsopogonophytes and stylonematophytes, porphyridiophytes, and rhodellophytes; Figure 4, panel B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Table S4- sheet 4 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This result addresses the concern that green genes might be artifacts of red algal undersampling.

claim: Ochrophytes branched as sister-groups to individual or multiple chlorophyte lineages in 51 of 67 trees of verified green origin.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of the HPPGs of verified green origin exhibited a strong bias toward chlorophyte origins. Ochrophytes branched as sister-groups to individual or multiple chlorophyte lineages in 51 of the 67 trees (Figure 4, panel C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: 56 of 67 green-origin HPPGs had BLAST top hits to chlorophyte lineages.
source: Similarly, we noted a strong predominance of chlorophyte lineages amongst BLAST top hits (56/67)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from BLAST analysis.

claim: Chlorophyte lineages correspond to approximately 25% of the green sequences in the libraries used.
source: despite the fact that these lineages only correspond to approximately 25% of the green sequences present in our libraries (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Table S4- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This contextualizes the bias toward chlorophyte hits.

claim: Only 16 single-gene trees of verified green origin recovered a sister-group relationship between ochrophytes and all green lineages.
source: In contrast, only 16 of the single-gene trees for HPPGs of verified green origin recovered a sister-group relationship between ochrophytes and all green lineages (chlorophytes and streptophytes)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: None of the single-gene trees recovered a specific sister-group relationship between ochrophytes and streptophytes.
source: none recovered a specific sister-group relationship between ochrophytes and streptophytes (Figure 4, panel C)
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Only 11 BLAST top hits of green-origin HPPGs were to streptophyte sequences.
source: and only 11 of the BLAST top hits were to streptophyte sequences (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Table S4- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from BLAST analysis.

claim: The majority of uniquely shared residues between ochrophytes and chlorophytes originated in a common ancestor of all chlorophytes or all chlorophytes excluding basal lineages (189/289 positions in observed analysis; 100/147 in earliest possible analysis).
source: In both analyses the majority of the uniquely shared residues were inferred to have originated in a common ancestor of all chlorophytes, or of all chlorophyte lineages excluding the basal Prasinoderma/ Nephroselmis sub-category (189/289 positions in observed analysis; 100/147 positions in the earliest possible analysis; Figure 4, panel D; Figure 4—figure supplement 4; Table S7- sheets 1, 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of uniquely shared residues.

claim: Gene families of red algal origin showed a stronger bias towards plastid-targeted proteins than green algal genes (chi-squared, p<1E−40).
source: We also observed a similar, though stronger, bias towards plastid-targeted proteins among the proteins of red algal origin (chi-squared, p<1E−40; Figure 4, panel E; Figure 4—figure supplement 5; Table S8- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This statistical result provides context for the green algal bias.

claim: Effectively complete core plastid metabolism pathways were identified within the ancestral HPPG dataset.
source: We identified effectively complete core plastid metabolism pathways within the ancestral HPPG dataset (Figure 5, panel A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table S9- sheet 1 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is stated and shown in figures and tables.

claim: In four cases (isopropylmalate synthase, sedoheptulose bisphosphatase, 3-dehydroquinate synthase, and shikimate kinase), lateral gene transfer and replacement events have occurred into individual ochrophyte lineages since their radiation.
source: In four cases (isopropylmalate synthase, sedoheptulose bisphosphatase, 3-dehydroquinate synthase, and shikimate kinase) lateral gene transfer and replacement events have occurred into individual ochrophyte lineages since their radiation, preventing identification of a single HPPG within the ancestral dataset (Figure 5, panel A; Figure 5—figure supplements 2–6).
evidence: This is stated and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There is very little evidence that individual categories of HPPG are associated with particular KOG annotations (chi-squared testing, p<0.05).
source: Consistent with this latter idea, we found very little evidence that individual categories of HPPG (i.e., red algal, green algal, prokaryotic or host origin) are associated with particular KOG annotations, as inferred by chi-squared testing (p<0.05) against a null hypothesis that all KOG families and classes are homogenously distributed across the ancestral HPPG dataset, independent of evolutionary origin (Figure 5, panel B; Figure 5—figure supplement 7; Table S9- sheet 2 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This statistical result supports functional mixing of proteins from different origins.

claim: Prokaryotic HPPGs are elevated in information storage and processing proteins, particularly those involved in translation.
source: The notable exceptions are prokaryotic HPPGs being elevated in information storage and processing proteins, particularly those involved in translation
evidence: This is an exception to the general pattern, identified by statistical testing.

claim: HPPGs of host origin were enriched in proteins involved in cellular processes and signalling relative to the ancestral HPPG set as a whole.
source: while HPPGs of host origin were enriched in proteins involved in cellular processes and signalling relative to the ancestral HPPG set as a whole (Figure 5, panel B; Figure 5—figure supplement 7; Table S9- sheet 2 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is identified by statistical testing.

claim: Of 313 pairs of biochemical neighbors identified in ancestral HPPGs, only 44 shared the same evolutionary origin, which is not different from random expectation (chi-squared test, p=0.541).
source: Of the 313 pairs of such biochemical neighbours identified in the ancestral HPPGs, only 44 shared the same evolutionary origin, which is no different than that which would be expected by chance (expected number 41.05; chi-squared test, p=0.541; Figure 5, panel C; Table S9- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016])
evidence: This statistical result shows no preference for same-origin proteins in metabolic pathways.

claim: There is no evidence that ancestral HPPG genes of any evolutionary origin had more similar expression dynamics to each other than to those of other evolutionary origins (ANOVA, p≤0.05).
source: We found no evidence that ancestral HPPG genes of any evolutionary origin had more similar expression dynamics to each other than to those of other evolutionary origins (ANOVA, p≤0.05; Figure 5, panel D; Figure 5—figure supplements 8 and 9; Table S10- sheet 5 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This statistical result shows functional integration across evolutionary origins.

claim: Seven chimeric proteins previously identified were found as orthologues within the ancestral HPPG dataset.
source: We identified orthologues of seven chimeric proteins identified in this study within our dataset, underlining their importance for the establishment of the ochrophyte plastid (Figure 6, panel A) (Méheust et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with reference to a previous study and shown in a figure.

claim: Chimerism events were identified in members of 42 ancestral HPPGs.
source: Using the taxonomic subdivisions erected for this study, we identified further chimerism events in members of 42 ancestral HPPGs (Figure 6, panel B; Table S9- sheet 1, sections 4, 5; Table S11 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Three HPPGs contain chimeric proteins formed through fusion of modules of prokaryotic origin to others of eukaryotic origin.
source: These include three HPPGs (e.g. NADH-ubiquinone dehydrogenase) in which chimeric proteins have formed through the fusion of modules of prokaryotic origin to others of eukaryotic origin
evidence: This is stated as a result of the chimerism analysis.

claim: Seven HPPGs contain chimeric proteins formed through fusion events between modules of red origin and modules of green origin.
source: and seven HPPGs (e.g. translation factor EF-3b, and an N6-adenine DNA methyltransferase) in which fusion events have occurred between modules of red origin and modules of green origin (Figure 6, panel B).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the chimerism analysis.

claim: Two chimeric proteins probably fused in the ochrophyte ancestor.
source: Amongst the chimeric proteins identified, we found two that probably fused in the ochrophyte ancestor (Figure 6, panels A, B).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic distribution and analysis.

claim: A bifunctional DHBP synthase/GTP cyclohydrolase II protein in ochrophytes has formed through fusion of a cyclohydrolase domain of probable host origin to a synthase domain of probable red algal or actinobacterial origin.
source: In one case, a bifunctional protein containing an N-terminal 3,4-dihydroxy-2-butanone 4-phosphate (DHBP) synthase and C-terminal GTP cyclohydrolase II protein, which performs two consecutive steps of riboflavin biosynthesis (Herz et al., 2000), has formed through the fusion of a cyclohydrolase domain of probable host origin to a synthase domain of probable red algal or actinobacterial origin (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated and shown in supplementary figures, with citation for the function.

claim: The ochrophyte bifunctional DHBP synthase/GTP cyclohydrolase protein has a topographically distinct domain arrangement compared to analogous proteins in bacteria, red algae and plants.
source: While bifunctional DHBP synthase/ GTP cyclohydrolase proteins are known in bacteria, red algae and plants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Herz et al., 2000), in these taxa the DHBP synthase domain is located at the protein C-terminus; thus, an analogous but topographically distinct fusion protein has evolved in ochrophytes.
evidence: This comparison is made with reference to other organisms and citations.

claim: A C-terminal plastid-targeted Tic20 subunit of red algal origin has become fused to an N-terminal EF-hand motif in ochrophytes.
source: In a second, previously reported case (Méheust et al., 2016), a C-terminal plastid-targeted Tic20 subunit of red algal origin has become fused to an N-terminal EF-hand motif, for which no clear evolutionary outgroup (to an e value of below 1 × 10−05) could be found (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated with reference to a previous study and shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Dual-targeting of proteins to plastids and mitochondria occurs extensively in plants.
source: As an exemplar system, we considered dual-targeting of proteins to plastids and mitochondria, which is known to occur extensively in plants (Xu et al., 2013; Duchêne et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dual-targeting has been documented in diatoms and other complex plastid lineages.
source: and has recently been documented in diatoms (Gile et al., 2015) and in other complex plastid lineages (Gile et al., 2015; Hirakawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Dual-targeting of histidyl- and prolyl-tRNA synthetase is a conserved feature across P. tricornutum, G. foliaceum, and N. gaditana.
source: In at least two cases (histidyl- and prolyl-tRNA synthetase) this dual-targeting is a conserved feature, as we identified the same fluorescence patterns both in P. tricornutum and using heterologous expression constructs from G. foliaceum and N. gaditana (Figure 7, panel A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally and shown in figures.

claim: 34 HPPGs passed conservation thresholds signifying an ancestral origin and are probably dual-targeted to plastids and mitochondria.
source: 34 of these HPPGs passed the conservation thresholds previously inferred to signify an ancestral origin (Table S12- sheet 1 [Dorrell et al., 2016]). Thus, dual-targeting is an ancestral feature of the ochrophyte plastid.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the in silico analysis.

claim: Of 15 putative ancestrally dual-targeted HPPGs with clear evolutionary origin, the majority (11/15; 73%) were of red algal origin.
source: 15 of the 34 putative ancestrally dual-targeted HPPGs were orthologous to HPPGs of clear evolutionary origin; of these, the majority (11/15; 73%) were of red algal, i.e., probable endosymbiont origin (Figure 7, panel B; Table S12- sheet 2 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Seven classes of tRNA synthetase in the ochrophyte ancestor are represented by only two genes, one cytosolic and one dual-targeted.
source: We identified seven classes of tRNA synthetase for which there were only two gene families in the ochrophyte ancestor, one corresponding to a cytosolic enzyme, and the other to an enzyme that was probably dual-targeted to both the mitochondria and plastid.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: In five cases of dual-targeted tRNA synthetases, the dual-targeted enzyme was of apparent red algal origin.
source: These include five cases in which the dual-targeted tRNA synthetase was of apparent red algal, i.e., endosymbiont origin (Figure 7, panel C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in a figure.

claim: In a majority (243/437) of trees where they could be assigned a clear origin, plastid-targeted proteins from haptophytes resolved at a position within the ochrophyte clade.
source: In a majority (243/437) of trees in which they could be assigned a clear origin, plastid-targeted proteins from haptophytes resolved at a position within the ochrophyte clade (Materials and methods; Figure 8, panel A; Table S4- sheet 5 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The proportion of haptophyte proteins that resolved within the ochrophytes was significantly greater than any other group except dinotoms (chi-squared, p<1×10−05).
source: Indeed, the proportion of haptophyte proteins that resolved within the ochrophytes was found to be significantly greater than any of the other groups except for dinotoms (chi-squared, p<1×10−05; Table S4- sheet 5 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This statistical result highlights the unique relationship between haptophytes and ochrophytes.

claim: Over half (100/178) of haptophyte plastid-targeted proteins that grouped with a specific ochrophyte lineage resolved with members of the hypogyristea.
source: We noted that the plastid-targeted haptophyte proteins of ochrophyte origin were biased towards specific origins, with over half of the proteins that grouped with a specific ochrophyte lineage (100/178) resolving with members of the hypogyristea (i.e., pelagophytes, dictyochophytes, and bolidophytes; Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Table S4- sheet 5 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing a specific bias.

claim: 53 ASAFind-generated HPPGs contained a majority of haptophyte sub-categories and at least one hypogyristean member but no other ochrophyte orthologues, which is significantly more than expected (chi-squared p=0.00013).
source: We found 53 ASAFind-generated HPPGs that contained a majority (≥2/3) of the haptophyte sub-categories and contained at least one member of the hypogyristea, but contained no other ochrophyte orthologues (Figure 8, panel B; Table S2- sheet 2, section 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016]). This was significantly more than would be expected (28.3, chi-squared p=0.00013)
evidence: This statistical result supports a specific relationship between haptophytes and hypogyristea.

claim: The greatest number (94) of haptophyte sequences resolved specifically with pelagophyte and dictyochophyte sequences in single-gene trees.
source: First, we tabulated the individual ochrophyte sub-categories identified in the first sister group to haptophyte sequences, of which the greatest number (94) resolved specifically with pelagophyte and dictyochophyte sequences, rather than with bolidophytes, non-hypogyristean lineages, or more ancestral nodes (Figure 8, panel C; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: For each haptophyte sub-category, at least 50% of sequences with evolutionarily consistent top hits resolved with pelagophytes or dictyochophytes.
source: In each case, at least 50% of the sequences that produced an evolutionarily consistent series of top hits resolved either with the pelagophytes or dictyochophytes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3; Table S13- sheet 4 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from BLAST analysis.

claim: The majority of haptophyte proteins of hypogyristean origin (65/100) clearly resolved within a broader HPPG containing multiple ochrophyte lineages in single-gene trees.
source: The majority of haptophyte proteins of hypogyristean origin in single-gene trees (65/100) clearly resolved within a broader HPPG containing multiple ochrophyte lineages
evidence: This is a quantitative result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The majority of haptophyte proteins with hypogyristean BLAST top hits and hypogyristean proteins with haptophyte BLAST top hits (48/86 sequences total) had next best BLAST hits against diatoms.
source: Moreover, the majority of haptophyte proteins with hypogyristean BLAST top hits, and hypogyristean proteins with haptophyte BLAST top hits (48/86 sequences total) had next best BLAST hits against diatoms (Figure 8—figure supplement 4, panel B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from BLAST analysis.

claim: A greater number of uniquely shared residues between haptophytes and ochrophytes were conserved with the common ancestor of hypogyristea and diatoms (139 residues) than specifically with pelagophytes and dictyochophytes (99 residues).
source: A greater number of the uniquely shared residues were conserved between the haptophytes and the common ancestor of hypogyristea and diatoms, than were specifically only shared with pelagophyte and dictyochophyte sequences, both per the latest possible origin (139 residues shared with hypogyristea and diatoms; 99 residues with pelagophytes and dictyochophytes; Figure 8, panel D; Table S7- sheets 2, 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016])
evidence: This is a quantitative result from residue analysis.

claim: A significantly larger proportion of ancestral haptophyte gene families of hypogyristean origin were predicted to be plastid-targeted than expected by random distribution (observed 43, expected 22.8, chi-squared p=2.2×10−05).
source: A significantly larger proportion of the ancestral haptophyte gene families of hypogyristean origin were predicted by ASAFind to be targeted to the plastid than would be expected by random distribution of the data (observed number 43, expected number 22.8, chi-squared p=2.2×10−05; Figure 8, panel E; Table S14- sheet 3 [Dorrell et al., 2016])
evidence: This statistical result supports an endosymbiotic origin for hypogyristean genes in haptophytes.

claim: A specific sister-group relationship between the cryptomonads and haptophytes was recovered with moderate to strong bootstrap support in both gene-rich and taxon-rich plastid genome trees.
source: A specific sister-group relationship between the cryptomonads and haptophytes was recovered, with moderate to strong bootstrap support, in both the gene-rich tree (Figure 9, panel A) and the taxon-rich tree (Figure 9, panel B).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis of plastid genomes.

claim: Both plastid genome trees strongly supported the monophyly of ochrophyte plastid genomes.
source: Both trees also strongly supported the monophyly of ochrophyte plastid genomes (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Alternative topology tests rejected any possibility that the haptophyte plastid originated within the ochrophytes (p≤0.05).
source: Alternative topology tests rejected any possibility that the haptophyte plastid originated within the ochrophytes (Figure 9—figure supplement 1; p≤0.05).
evidence: This is a result from statistical topology testing.

claim: Only three residues in the gene-rich plastid genome alignment were uniquely shared among all four haptophytes and the sole pelagophyte/dictyochophyte representative.
source: Finally, we found only three residues in the alignment that were uniquely shared among all four haptophytes and the sole representative of pelagophytes and dictyochophytes (Aureococcus) in the gene-rich dataset
evidence: This is a quantitative result from residue analysis.

claim: No residues were shared between a majority of haptophytes and at least one pelagophyte or dictyochophyte sequence in the taxon-rich plastid genome dataset.
source: and no residues that were shared between a majority of the haptophytes and at least one pelagophyte or dictyochophyte sequence in the taxon-rich dataset (Figure 8, panel C; Table S17- sheet 4 [Dorrell et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from residue analysis.

claim: The haptophyte plastid genome structure and content are dissimilar to hypogyristean plastid genomes.
source: Furthermore, the structure and content of haptophyte and hypogyristean plastid genomes are dissimilar: for example, haptophyte plastids possess an rpl36 gene that has been laterally acquired from a bacterial donor and is shared with cryptomonad plastids but absent from ochrophytes (Rice and Palmer, 2006), and ochrophyte plastids no longer retain genes encoding the plastid division machinery proteins minD and minE, which remain plastid-encoded in haptophytes and cryptomonads (de Vries and Gould, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural differences.

claim: Sequenced pelagophyte plastids have a reduced coding content compared to other photosynthetic ochrophytes, cryptomonads and haptophytes, and have secondarily lost the plastid inverted repeat.
source: Finally, extant haptophyte plastids have comparatively large plastid genomes and possess a conventional quadripartite structure (Green, 2011), whereas sequenced pelagophyte plastids (the harmful coastal species Aureococcus anophagefferens and Aureoumbra lagunensis, and an uncultured member of the predominantly open ocean genus Pelagomonas) all have a reduced coding content compared to other photosynthetic ochrophytes, cryptomonads and haptophytes, and have secondarily lost the plastid inverted repeat (Worden et al., 2012; Ong et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with citations to genomic studies.
